claims.text: The initial material is a homogenized, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy.
Anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr is primarily governed by internal stresses generated by thermal-expansion mismatch during thermal cycling.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch internal stresses alter dislocation activity.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch internal stresses alter the alloy's elastic response.
Different expansion and contraction rates of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr atoms generate residual internal stresses during thermal cycling.
The induced internal stresses modify dislocation glide.
The induced internal stresses modify dislocation climb.
The induced internal stresses modify the effective stiffness of the matrix.
The proposed internal-stress mechanism can unify the reported changes in creep, hardness, and elastic moduli.
Thermally cycled samples will have greater low-temperature yield strength than as-homogenized, uncycled samples.
Thermally cycled samples will have greater low-temperature hardness than as-homogenized, uncycled samples.
Thermally cycled samples will typically have reduced high-temperature creep resistance relative to as-homogenized, uncycled samples.
Temperature-dependent variations in elastic moduli will correlate with the magnitude of induced internal stresses.
Thermal-expansion mismatch is expected to govern the stated behavior from 293 K to 1250 °C.
At very low temperatures, thermal-expansion mismatch is minimal.
Outside the proposed temperature range, other processes may overshadow the thermal-expansion-mismatch effect.
Short-range ordering or nanoscale phase instabilities may contribute concurrently to the observed behavior.
